item.title: How to Read a Water Meter (and Know If Its Accurate)
item.description:
Quick Answer

Water meters measure in cubic feet or gallons: Read the first 4-5 numbers (black on white) to get your usage, then subtract the previous reading. Most residential usage is 80-150 gallons per person daily ($40-80/month typical).

  • Fact: A running toilet can waste 200-400 gallons daily, adding $50-100 to monthly bills
  • Action: Check your meter while all water is off - if it’s still moving, you have a leak

For more detail, see Understanding Utility Bills.

item.title: Is Your Toilet Running? A Simple Leak Test (and How It Shows Up on Your Water Bill)
item.description:
Quick Answer: Is Your Toilet Running?

A running toilet can waste 200–400 gallons a day and add $50–$100+ a month to your water bill (U.S. EPA WaterSense estimate). Test it in 10 minutes: drop 10 drops of food coloring in the tank, wait 10–15 minutes without flushing; if color appears in the bowl, the flapper is leaking.

Run the 10-Minute Dye Test

The dye test is the fastest way to confirm a toilet leak without any tools. It isolates the flapper, which causes the majority of running-toilet problems.

item.title: What Is CCF on a Water Bill? (Cubic Feet Explained in Plain English)
item.description:
Quick Answer

CCF means "hundred cubic feet" — 1 CCF equals 748 gallons of water. A typical household uses about 2–4 CCF per person per month; if your number is well above that range, a hidden leak (most often a running toilet) is the usual reason. CCF is just the volume unit your bill uses — the fee comes from the rate your utility charges per CCF.
